paragraphs: 14 Then Laban declared, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.”
After Jacob had stayed with him a month, 15 Laban said to him, “Just because you are my relative, should you work for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be.”

16 Now Laban had two daughters; the older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel. 17 Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful. 18 Since Jacob loved Rachel, he answered, “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.”
19 Laban replied, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” 20 So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her.
21 Finally Jacob said to Laban, “Grant me my wife, for my time is complete, and I want to sleep with her.”

22 So Laban invited all the men of that place and prepared a feast. 23 But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her. 24 And Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maidservant.
25 When morning came, there was Leah! “What have you done to me?” Jacob said to Laban. “Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?”

26 Laban replied, “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older. 27 Finish this week’s celebration, and we will give you the younger one in return for another seven years of work.”

28 And Jacob did just that. He finished the week’s celebration, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. 29 Laban also gave his servant girl Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant.
30 Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years.

context_lines: After Jacob has stayed a month, Laban asks what wages he should receive for his work. Jacob loves Rachel, the younger daughter, and offers seven years of service for her. His love makes the years seem short, and when the agreed time is complete he asks to marry her.

Laban prepares a feast but brings Leah to Jacob that evening. In the morning Jacob discovers the substitution and confronts him. Laban appeals to a local custom of marrying the older daughter first—an explanation he had not included when agreeing to Jacob's service for Rachel.

Laban offers Rachel as well after Leah's wedding week, in return for another seven years of work. Jacob agrees, completes the week, and marries Rachel before beginning the further service. He does not wait another seven years to receive her. Zilpah is given to Leah as a maidservant, and Bilhah to Rachel; both women will become important in the family story.

The closing statement exposes the coming difficulty: Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah. The man who deceived his father by taking his brother's place has now been deceived through the substitution of an older sister for a younger one. Leah enters a marriage in which she is not the woman her husband wanted, and that unequal affection will shape the household.
common_interpretation_lines: A common Christian reading notices the reversal: Jacob, who deceived Isaac, now experiences another person's deception himself. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 29:25–27](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) see a lesson in this while still treating Laban's conduct as wrong and the resulting multiple marriages as a source of trouble.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: Jacob's experience belongs alongside the Bible's larger teaching that God can train His people through painful circumstances. [Hebrews 12:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/12.htm) describes the Father's discipline as serving His children's good and growth in holiness. It does not explicitly identify this wedding as such a lesson, but the reversal invites Jacob—and the reader—to confront what deception does to another person.

The following account also directs attention to God's care for the unloved Leah. Her pain matters in its own right, alongside what Jacob may learn from his experience. God's work in a flawed household includes seeing the person whose pain other people have created.
